segments.t: At the agency, Gabriel finds a creative solution for client Norman Thavaud, who desperately needs an earlier driving test date. A fan named Violaine agrees to swap slots in exchange for meeting the star and taking photos. Listen to the conversation in French first.
Salut Norman! C'est le plus beau jour de ma vie.
Elle veut quelque chose de plus personnel.
Let's walk through the conversation step by step.
'I found someone to swap with you.' Built from 'some one' fused with an apostrophe, that compound means 'someone', followed by 'for' plus 'to swap' to show purpose.
'What is her name?' Taken word-for-word, Norman asks 'how she calls herself', keeping everyday spoken order after 'how' in French.
'Her name is Violaine.' Answering with the same 'she calls herself' frame is the standard way you'd say someone's name in French.
'Does she want money?' Literally 'silver', the closing term is what you'll hear for 'money', introduced by a 'some' marker before its opening vowel.
'No, just a selfie.' Modern speakers borrow 'selfie' straight from English, pairing it with 'a' in its male form in French.
'When do I take the test?' Watch the exam false friend: 'pass' a test in French means 'sit' or 'take' it—not necessarily pass! Casual speech tucks 'when' right at the end.
'Tomorrow, after we see Audiard.' Linking a full clause after 'after' requires adding 'that' in French, clipped here before casual 'one' meaning 'we'.
'Perfect. That is good news.' A single piece of news is countable in French—literally 'a good new thing'—right after the cognate 'perfect'.
Salut Norman! C'est le plus beau jour de ma vie.
'Hi Norman! This is the best day of my life.' Putting 'the most handsome' in front of 'day' builds 'the best day', linked to 'my life' by 'of' in French.
'That is kind. Thank you very much.' Adding 'a lot' directly after 'thanks' gives you 'thank you very much'—never insert 'very' there in French.
'Shall we take this photo together?' Photographers in French say 'make a photo' instead of 'take a photo', turning the suggestion into a question through rising pitch.
'Smile for the photo!' Ending in '-ez', this polite command addresses both Gabriel and Norman at once, built from 'under-laugh' to mean 'smile'.
'Violaine, we are done. Thank you!' Literally 'it is finished', this crisp cognate expression politely wraps up a meeting or session.
'Is there a problem?' Built from 'it there has', that three-piece opener means 'there is'—and rising pitch turns it into 'is there?'.
Elle veut quelque chose de plus personnel.

'She wants something more personal.' Describing 'something' in French calls for a tiny 'of' bridge before 'more personal'. Now let's listen to the whole scene again at normal speed, and see how much more you catch.
Salut Norman! C'est le plus beau jour de ma vie.
Elle veut quelque chose de plus personnel.
With Norman's exam safely rescheduled, Gabriel must now manage an overenthusiastic fan who refuses to leave without a lock of hair. Listen to the French dialogue one more time. See you next time!
